learningObjectives.title: Magnetic fields, permanent and induced magnets
Electromagnets and the magnetic effect of a current
The motor effect and Fleming's left-hand rule
Force on a current-carrying conductor (F = BIl)

questions.q: Which of these materials is magnetic?
questions.explain: Iron, along with steel, cobalt and nickel, is a magnetic material that is attracted to magnets.

questions.q: Outside a bar magnet, in which direction do magnetic field lines point?
options: From south pole to north pole
From north pole to south pole
Always towards the centre of the magnet
questions.explain: By convention, magnetic field lines run from the north pole to the south pole outside the magnet.

questions.q: A piece of unmagnetised iron is brought near a magnet. What kind of force acts between them?
options: Attraction or repulsion depending on which pole is used
questions.explain: The iron becomes an induced magnet, and the force between a magnet and an induced magnet is always attractive.

questions.q: What happens when two like magnetic poles are brought close together?
questions.explain: Like poles (north-north or south-south) repel, while unlike poles attract.

questions.q: Where is the magnetic field of a bar magnet strongest?
options: In the middle of the magnet
The field has the same strength everywhere
questions.explain: The field is strongest at the poles, shown by the field lines being closest together there.

questions.q: A plotting compass is placed in a magnetic field. What does its needle do?
options: Points to the nearest heavy object
Aligns with the direction of the magnetic field
questions.explain: A compass needle is a small magnet that lines up with the field, which is also why compasses show that the Earth has a magnetic field generated by its core.

questions.q: What is the unit of magnetic flux density?
questions.explain: Magnetic flux density B is measured in tesla (T), where 1 T represents a strong field.

questions.q: In Fleming's left-hand rule, what does the First finger represent?
questions.explain: The First finger points in the direction of the magnetic Field (north to south).

questions.q: In Fleming's left-hand rule, what does the second (middle) finger represent?
questions.explain: The seCond finger points in the direction of the conventional Current (positive to negative).

questions.q: In Fleming's left-hand rule, what does the thumb represent?
options: The force (or motion) on the conductor
questions.explain: The thumb points in the direction of the thrust, that is the force or resulting motion of the wire.

questions.q: Which change would increase the strength of an electromagnet?
options: Decreasing the current in the coil
Adding an iron core inside the coil
questions.explain: An iron core, more turns of wire, or a larger current all increase the strength of an electromagnet.

questions.q: What is the magnetic field like inside a current-carrying solenoid?
options: Strong and uniform, similar to a bar magnet
Weak and pointing towards the wire
questions.explain: Inside a solenoid the field is strong and uniform, and the overall field pattern resembles that of a bar magnet.

questions.q: When is the force on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field equal to zero?
options: When the wire is at 90° to the field
When the wire is parallel to the field
When the current is at a maximum
questions.explain: The force is zero when the current is parallel to the field and greatest when it is at 90° (perpendicular) to the field.

questions.q: A wire of length 0.2 m carries a current of 5 A at 90° to a field of flux density 0.4 T. What is the force on the wire? (F = BIl)
A 0.5 m wire carrying 3 A experiences a force of 0.6 N at 90° to a magnetic field. What is the flux density? (F = BIl)
A 0.4 m wire in a 0.5 T field (at 90°) experiences a force of 2 N. What is the current? (F = BIl)
In the motor effect, what happens to the direction of the force if the direction of the current is reversed?
questions.explain: Reversing either the current or the field reverses the direction of the force, as predicted by Fleming's left-hand rule.

questions.q: Which device makes use of an electromagnet?
options: A scrapyard crane for lifting cars
questions.explain: Electromagnets are used in devices such as scrapyard cranes, relays and electric bells because they can be switched on and off.

questions.q: What is the key difference between a permanent magnet and an induced magnet?
options: A permanent magnet produces its own field; an induced magnet is only magnetic when in a field
An induced magnet is always stronger than a permanent magnet
A permanent magnet is only magnetic near the Earth's poles
There is no difference between them
questions.explain: A permanent magnet produces its own magnetic field, whereas an induced magnet becomes magnetic only while placed in a magnetic field and loses most magnetism when removed.

questions.q: A student wants the maximum possible force on a current-carrying wire placed between two magnets. How should the wire be arranged relative to the magnetic field?
options: It makes no difference to the force
questions.explain: The force is greatest when the wire (current) is perpendicular to the magnetic field.
